analysis.one_liner: Permanently protects the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness, barring oil drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 99 cosponsors, including 7 Republicans, but died in the House Resources Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add about 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska — the '1002 Area' coastal plain — to the National Wilderness Preservation System [S3]. Wilderness designation is the strongest protection federal law offers: it permanently bars roads, construction, and industrial development, which would foreclose drilling for oil under the refuge's coastal plain [S3]. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who holds the refuge as public property. Wilderness designation would keep roughly 1.56 million acres of Alaska's coastal tundra — calving ground for the Porcupine caribou herd and habitat for migratory birds — undeveloped permanently, rather than leaving it open to a future oil leasing program [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill designates approximately 1,559,538 acres in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge as wilderness and a component of the National Wilderness Preservation System, acting under the Wilderness Act, which permanently bars development of designated land [S3].
The land in question is the refuge's 1002 Area, the coastal plain repeatedly studied for its oil potential; designation would settle the question in favor of protection rather than drilling [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies lose the chance to explore and drill in one of the largest untapped onshore areas on federal land, and Alaska's petroleum-centered economy loses the jobs, revenue, and royalties that development advocates projected [S3]. The federal treasury would forgo any future bids and royalties from leasing there.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies and Alaska's petroleum economy

drawbacks.text: The cost is permanent. Wilderness designation cannot be undone by a later Congress in practice, so it forecloses domestic oil production from a major prospect forever — a real cost in energy supply, jobs, and royalties that drilling supporters in Alaska and the oil industry would bear [S3].

The bill designated the land outright with no study or phased approach, skipping the environmental review and hearing process that a lands bill of this size normally goes through before enactment [S3][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a permanent, irreversible protection of a unique Arctic ecosystem against forgone oil development whose value is uncertain and whose environmental risk, by the bill's logic, is not. The design choice is blunt — no hearing, no study, no compromise — which is part of why it made no progress even with 99 cosponsors. For people who weigh intact wilderness over potential oil supply, the trade favors protection; for Alaska's development economy it is a pure loss.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 1995, referred to the House Resources Committee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 1997 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Vento introduced the bill on February 21, 1995; it was referred to the House Committee on Resources [S5].
It accumulated 99 cosponsors — 91 Democrats, 7 Republicans, and 1 Independent — within its first weeks [S4].

On March 16, 1995 the committee requested an executive comment from the Interior Department, the last action the bill ever received; it died in committee when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies and Alaska officials who favor opening the Arctic Refuge to drilling kept the coastal plain's status undecided, preserving the option to pursue drilling in future Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drilling advocates and the oil industry

for.name: Rep. Bruce Vento
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the initial cosponsor list

against.name: Rep. Don Young
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup, and was a leading advocate for opening the Arctic Refuge to oil drilling instead

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Prospective developer of the refuge's coastal plain
against.what_they_did: Opposed wilderness designation for the 1002 Area and supported the new majority's push to open it to drilling

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 91 of 99 cosponsors — with only 7 of the House's 230 Republicans signing on, in a Congress where Republicans had just taken majority control of the House and its committees.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar drilling in the Arctic Refuge coastal plain, one of the largest untapped federal oil prospects, removing a future source of company revenue. Its gain (protection of public land) would come at their expense, so its interest runs against the preservation outcome the bill delivers to the public.

industries.industry: Alaska petroleum economy and state government
industries.note: Alaska's government and its petroleum-dependent economy had long sought coastal plain development for jobs and royalties; wilderness designation would eliminate that option permanently.

Downstream businesses tied to intact Arctic ecosystems — caribou herds migratory birds and subsistence and recreation economies — benefit from permanent protection of the calving grounds the 1002 Area contains.
